subsections.title: Introduction to Operations and Finance Management

content.text: Good operations and finance management is the foundation for strong education at Eduversal Partner Schools. The main mission of every school is student learning and development. But the quality of that education depends on sound operational systems, careful financial management, well-maintained facilities and well-managed resources. This section gives principals full guidance on operational and financial leadership in the special Yayasan-Eduversal partnership model.

content.title: 13.1.1 The Role of Operations and Finance in Educational Excellence
content.text:
Operations and finance are not side tasks for administrators. They are strategic tools that support the school's educational mission. Every decision about the budget, facility maintenance, technology or buying resources directly affects the quality of teaching and learning. When operational systems run smoothly and money is managed openly, teachers can focus on teaching. Students can learn in safe, well-equipped spaces. The whole school community can work toward excellence without distraction.

At Eduversal Partner Schools, operational excellence means several things. Cambridge curriculum materials arrive on time. Science laboratories are properly equipped and maintained. Technology infrastructure supports digital learning. Transportation runs safely and reliably. Boarding facilities (where applicable) give students a caring place for their all-round development. Financial resources are allocated strategically to support the School Improvement Plan (see Section 4 for strategic planning frameworks).

content.title: 13.1.2 Dual Accountability Framework: Yayasan and Eduversal Partnership
content.text: School leaders in the Eduversal partnership model need to understand how operations and finance are governed. This structure is a careful balance between two partners. The Yayasan (foundation) owns the school. Eduversal provides management expertise and quality assurance.

content.title: Yayasan Responsibilities
content.text: The Yayasan is the legal owner of the school. It holds final authority over major financial decisions, property ownership and strategic direction. The Yayasan Board approves annual budgets and reviews financial performance. It authorizes large capital expenditures. It makes sure the school follows Indonesian foundation law (UU No. 16/2001 concerning Foundations, as amended by UU No. 28/2004, and PP No. 63/2008). The Yayasan also has fiduciary responsibility (a legal duty of care) for the school's assets and long-term sustainability.

content.title: Eduversal Management Support
content.text: Eduversal gives full management support through the General Manager (GM) or Foundation Representative (FR). The GM/FR is the operational leader, with full authority over day-to-day management. This includes curriculum delivery, student guidance and counseling, character education, financial operations and human resource management. Eduversal also provides Quality Management System (QMS) components. These include EduNav platform access, EASE assessments, DTP professional development programs and the Appraisal Program. They improve operational efficiency and educational quality across the partner school network.

content.title: Principal's Role in This Framework
content.text: The Principal works within this dual accountability structure and has clearly defined responsibilities. The Principal provides educational leadership and manages the quality of teaching and learning. The Principal also oversees student welfare and discipline, supervises academic staff and carries out the approved budget. For operational and financial matters, the Principal usually reports to the GM/FR and works closely with them. The GM/FR in turn coordinates with both the Yayasan Board and Eduversal. Section 1 (Governance Charter) describes this structure in full.

content.title: 13.1.3 Principal's Operational and Financial Leadership Responsibilities
content.text: As the educational leader and senior administrator at school level, the Principal has significant operational and financial responsibilities. However, the Principal must carry these out within the governance framework set by the Yayasan-Eduversal partnership.

content.title: Financial Stewardship
content.text: The Principal takes an active part in developing the annual budget. The Principal gives input based on educational priorities and resource needs. Once the budget is approved, the Principal manages spending within approved categories and spending authority limits. The Principal also monitors budget performance against plans, spots possible variances early and recommends adjustments when needed. The Principal makes sure that money is allocated fairly and strategically to support educational outcomes. This matters most for priority areas such as curriculum materials, teaching resources, professional development, student support services and technology infrastructure.

content.title: Operational Oversight
content.text: The Principal holds final responsibility for school operations that directly affect the educational program. This includes making sure facilities are safe, clean and good for learning. It includes working with maintenance staff to fix issues promptly, and overseeing technology systems that support teaching and administration. It includes managing school transportation (where applicable), with a focus on student safety. It includes supervising boarding operations (for boarding schools), with a focus on student welfare. It also includes making sure the school complies with Indonesian health, safety and operational regulations.

content.title: Resource Management
content.text: To manage resources well, the Principal needs to balance competing priorities, make evidence-based decisions and stay transparent. The Principal oversees the purchase of curriculum materials and educational resources. The Principal manages the inventory of textbooks, supplies and equipment, and works with vendors and service providers. The Principal makes sure resources reach classrooms, and monitors how they are used to get the most benefit for student learning.

content.title: Staff Management
content.text: Section 12 covers detailed staff lifecycle procedures. Operational management also includes the Principal's responsibility for operational staff (maintenance, administrative and support personnel), in addition to academic staff. This includes supervising performance, dealing with operational issues, making sure there are enough staff, and building a culture of excellent service across all departments.

content.title: 13.1.4 Integration with EduNav Platform for Operational Excellence
content.text: EduNav is Eduversal's full School Information System. It is the central platform for operational and financial management across all partner schools. The Principal must become skilled in using EduNav for many operational functions.

content.title: Financial Management Features
content.text: EduNav simplifies the whole financial workflow with its online system for submitting and approving expenses. All purchase requests, reimbursements and spending approvals go through EduNav. This creates transparency and keeps proper internal controls in place. The system tracks budget performance in real time and produces financial reports automatically. It alerts principals to budget variances and keeps a complete audit trail of all financial transactions.

content.title: Operational Monitoring
content.text: EduNav also goes beyond finance. Its dashboards show key operational performance indicators (KPIs), facility maintenance schedules and work orders, and asset inventories and tracking systems. They also show vendor contracts and performance records, and compliance documents for regulatory requirements.

content.title: Evidence Repository
content.text: For accreditation (CIS/WASC and BAN-S/M), EduNav is the central store for operational evidence and documents. Principals can easily organize and find financial reports, operational policies and procedures, maintenance records, vendor agreements and insurance certificates. They can also find safety inspection reports and other compliance documents. This greatly reduces administrative work during accreditation visits and regulatory audits.

content.title: 13.1.5 Compliance Context: Indonesian Regulations and International Standards
content.text: Operations and finance management at Eduversal Partner Schools must meet several regulatory and accreditation frameworks at the same time. Each framework has its own requirements.

content.title: Indonesian Regulatory Requirements
content.text: Indonesian law sets specific requirements for school operations and financial management. UU No. 16/2001 as amended by UU No. 28/2004, together with PP No. 63/2008, governs how foundations operate and account for money. Labor law (UU No. 13/2003 and later amendments) regulates employment practices, pay and benefits. Building codes and safety regulations (Peraturan Menteri PUPR) set standards for building, maintaining and using facilities. Tax regulations require correct handling of income tax withholding (PPh), value-added tax (PPN) and annual tax reporting (SPT). BAN-S/M accreditation standards include specific operational and financial criteria. Schools must meet these criteria to gain national accreditation status.

content.title: International Accreditation Standards
content.text: CIS (Council of International Schools) Domain G (Premises, facilities, technology systems and auxiliary services) covers buildings and physical resources. It requires schools to show that facilities, equipment and materials support the educational program. CIS Domain B, standard B3, covers educational and financial strategic and operational planning. It requires transparent budgeting, responsible financial management and long-term financial planning. WASC (Western Association of Schools and Colleges) reviews resource management as part of its full school review. It looks at how resources are allocated to support student learning outcomes.

content.title: Cambridge Centre Requirements
content.text: As registered Cambridge International Schools, partner schools must maintain certain operational standards. These include secure storage and handling of examination materials, and suitable facilities for practical examinations (especially in science subjects). They also include reliable internet access to the Cambridge School Support Hub, and proper management of Cambridge digital resources and teaching materials.

content.title: Integrated Compliance Approach
content.text: Good principals do not treat these frameworks as separate burdens. They build compliance into routine operational systems. This section shows how to meet all requirements at the same time. It uses shared policies, procedures and documentation systems that satisfy Indonesian, international and Cambridge standards.

content.title: 13.1.6 Cultural Context: Indonesian School Operations
content.text: Operations and finance management in Indonesian international schools needs cultural awareness. Schools need to adapt to local contexts while keeping international standards.

content.title: Tropical Climate Considerations
content.text: Indonesia's tropical climate creates specific operational challenges that principals must plan for. Monsoon seasons (usually October-March) need preparation for flooding, water coming into buildings and transportation disruptions. High humidity affects building maintenance, how long equipment lasts and document storage. Warm temperatures all year mean the school needs reliable air conditioning, especially in computer labs and examination rooms. Principals must include climate-specific preventive maintenance, emergency preparedness procedures and budget allocations for climate-related challenges.

content.title: Cultural Business Practices
content.text: Indonesian business culture values relationship-building (the gotong royong spirit of mutual cooperation). It also values respectful communication with vendors and service providers, patience in negotiation and long-term partnerships. Principals should build strong relationships with local vendors, engage respectfully with community suppliers, understand Indonesian negotiation norms, and balance costs with keeping good relationships.

content.title: Islamic Context (for Islamic Boarding Schools)
content.text: Schools with Islamic boarding programs need specific operational arrangements. These include keeping prayer facilities (musholla or masjid) maintained and clean, and systems for buying and preparing halal food. They also include Ramadan schedule changes (including sahur and iftar meal services) and room for religious observance in daily operations. Finally, they include building Islamic values into facility design and operational policies.

content.title: Regulatory Environment
content.text: Understanding Indonesian regulatory culture is essential. Government processes need complete documents and can take time. Allow plenty of lead time, keep records up to date and communicate early with regulatory authorities. Principals should do four things. Keep good relationships with local education offices (Dinas Pendidikan). Keep regulatory documents current and organized. Plan ahead for bureaucratic processes. Ask Eduversal for support when facing regulatory challenges.

content.title: 13.1.7 Key Principles for Operational and Financial Excellence
content.text: Several fundamental principles should guide principals' approach to operations and finance management:

content.title: Transparency and Accountability
content.text: All financial decisions should be documented, justified and open to appropriate review. Operational systems should keep clear audit trails, involve appropriate oversight and show responsible care of the school's resources. Families, the Yayasan and Eduversal entrust these resources to the school.

content.title: Mission Alignment
content.text: Every operational decision should ultimately serve the educational mission. With this focus, operational efficiency never becomes a goal in itself. It stays a way to reach educational excellence. When principals weigh competing resource priorities, they should ask: "How does this support student learning and wellbeing?"

content.title: Preventive Rather Than Reactive
content.text: Good operational management sees problems coming before they happen. Preventive maintenance avoids expensive emergency repairs. Early budget monitoring avoids overspending crises. Regular safety inspections prevent accidents. Strategic planning prevents resource shortages. Time spent on systematic, preventive approaches pays back well, again and again.

content.title: Continuous Improvement
content.text: Operations and finance management should follow the same continuous improvement mindset used in teaching and learning. Regular reviews of operational efficiency and benchmarking with other Eduversal partner schools build operational excellence. So do asking stakeholders for feedback and being willing to innovate and adapt systems.

content.title: Collaboration and Communication
content.text: Good operational management needs collaboration with many people. These include the GM/FR, the Yayasan Board, Eduversal support services and operational staff teams. They also include academic staff who use resources and facilities, and external vendors and service providers. Clear, early communication prevents misunderstandings, builds trust and makes coordinated action possible.

content.title: 13.1.8 Structure of This Section

content.text: Each subsection explains not only "what" and "why" but also "how". It gives practical procedures, templates, decision-making frameworks and concrete examples from Indonesian international schools.

content.title: 13.1.9 Conclusion
content.text:
Operations and finance management may seem like technical, administrative work far from the core work of teaching and learning. In reality, they are the basic infrastructure that makes educational excellence possible. A principal who masters operational and financial leadership creates the right conditions. Teachers can teach well, students can learn with joy, and the whole school community can pursue its mission without unnecessary obstacles or distractions.

The guidance in this section reflects Eduversal's commitment to supporting principals. It gives practical, full frameworks for operational excellence that fit the local context. It combines Indonesian regulatory compliance, international accreditation standards, Cambridge requirements and proven management practices. In this way, Eduversal Partner Schools can achieve both operational efficiency and educational impact. These are the marks of truly excellent international schools.

content.text: Good financial planning and budget management are basic to a school's long-term health and educational quality. The annual budget is more than an accounting task. It shows the school's strategic priorities and educational mission in money terms. This section gives full guidance on budget development, the approval process, revenue management and spending controls. It applies within the Yayasan-Eduversal partnership framework.

content.title: Key Evidence and Artifacts — Financial Planning and Budget Management
13.2.1 Annual Budget Development Process
content.text: At Eduversal Partner Schools, the annual budget process follows a set timeline. It involves several stakeholders. This keeps the budget in line with educational priorities, legal and regulatory requirements, and long-term financial health.

content.title: Budget Development Timeline and Key Milestones
content.text:
The budget cycle usually starts 4-6 months before the academic year begins. In Indonesian schools, the academic year usually runs July-June. A recommended timeline is:

**January-February:** Initial budget planning starts. The Principal and GM/Foundation Representative review how the current year's budget has performed. They identify priorities to carry over and analyze enrollment projections for the coming year. They also assess facility and resource needs. They collect input from department heads and coordinators about the resources each program needs.

**March:** Draft budget preparation. The GM/Foundation Representative prepares the draft Rancangan Anggaran Belanja (RAB), or annual budget plan. The GM/Foundation Representative does this in consultation with Eduversal and with the Principal's active participation. The draft includes enrollment projections and educational program priorities from the School Improvement Plan (See Section 4.2.2). It also includes staffing needs, facility maintenance needs, technology infrastructure investments, curriculum resources and materials, and contingency reserves.

**April:** Yayasan review and feedback. The draft RAB goes to the Yayasan Board for evaluation. The Yayasan reviews budget assumptions, revenue projections, major spending categories, alignment with strategic priorities, and financial sustainability indicators. The Yayasan may ask for changes, extra justifications, or alternative scenarios.

**May:** Budget finalization and approval. The GM and Principal revise the draft budget as needed, based on Yayasan feedback. The Yayasan Board formally approves the final budget, and the GM/Foundation Representative signs it. This shows mutual agreement between both Yayasan parties (the local foundation and Eduversal). The approved budget then becomes the operating financial plan for the academic year.

**June:** Budget communication and preparation for implementation. The approved budget is shared with relevant stakeholders, including department heads, coordinators and finance staff. Budget allocations are uploaded into the EduNav system. Procurement plans are finalized for major purchases needed at the start of the academic year.

content.title: Stakeholder Involvement Throughout the Process
content.text:
Good budget development needs real input from several perspectives:

The Principal gives educational leadership input. The Principal identifies program priorities, resource needs for teaching and learning, student support needs, and professional development investments. The Principal makes sure the budget supports the School Improvement Plan goals and student learning outcome priorities.

The GM/Foundation Representative leads the budget process and brings together input from all departments. The GM/Foundation Representative makes sure the budget follows Yayasan policies and Eduversal standards. The GM/Foundation Representative also coordinates with Eduversal on QMS (Quality Management System) budget items: DTP programs, Appraisal Program, EduNav platform fees and EASE assessments. The GM/Foundation Representative negotiates with the Yayasan Board and keeps overall financial accountability.

The Yayasan Board carries out fiduciary oversight. It reviews and approves the proposed budget and makes sure the school stays financially sustainable. It authorizes major capital expenditures and monitors how the budget is used during the year.

Department Heads and Coordinators identify the resources their areas need. They propose budget allocations for their programs. They commit to managing resources well within approved budgets.

The Finance Team gives technical support in budget preparation. It makes sure the budget format meets accounting standards and regulatory requirements. It keeps historical financial data for reference. It also prepares financial projections and scenarios.

content.title: Strategic Plan Alignment
content.text: The annual budget must reflect and fund the priorities in the school's 5-year Strategic Plan and annual School Improvement Plan. (See Section 4 for full guidance on strategic planning.) Each major budget category should link to specific strategic goals. For example, suppose the Strategic Plan prioritizes stronger STEAM education. In that case, the budget should include money for science laboratory equipment, robotics materials, teacher professional development in STEAM pedagogy, and related technology infrastructure. This strategic alignment means money drives educational improvement, instead of repeating past spending patterns.

content.title: Budget Categories and Structure
content.text:
Eduversal Partner Schools usually organize budgets into major categories. These categories help with both financial management and educational planning:

Personnel Costs are the largest budget category, usually 50-70% of total spending. This includes teacher salaries and benefits, administrative staff pay, operational staff wages, and professional development allocations. It also includes payroll taxes and mandatory contributions (BPJS Kesehatan, BPJS Ketenagakerjaan).

Operational Expenses cover day-to-day school operations. These include utilities (electricity, water, internet), facility maintenance and repairs, cleaning and sanitation supplies, and office supplies and materials. They also include transportation operations (if applicable) and food services for boarding schools (if applicable).

Curriculum Resources fund the educational program directly. These include Cambridge textbooks and digital resources, library materials and subscriptions, and science laboratory supplies and equipment. They also include art and music supplies, physical education equipment, and technology for teaching and learning (educational software, devices).

Facilities and Infrastructure cover the needs of buildings and grounds. These include major maintenance projects, facility upgrades and renovations, furniture and equipment replacement, security systems, and landscaping and grounds maintenance.

Technology Infrastructure supports digital learning and administration. It includes hardware purchases and upgrades, software licensing, network infrastructure and bandwidth, and EduNav platform fees. It also includes cybersecurity measures and IT support services.

Student Activities and Programs add to the educational experience. They include extracurricular activities, student competitions and olympiads, field trips and educational excursions, and student welfare programs. They also include co-curricular programs aligned with School Learning Outcomes.

Quality Management System (QMS) Costs cover Eduversal partnership services. These include DTP professional development programs, Appraisal Program fees, EASE standardized assessments, EduNav platform subscription, and coordination of Eduversal support services.

Contingency Reserve covers unexpected events and emergencies. Best practice recommends keeping a contingency reserve of 5-10% of the operating budget. It pays for unexpected repairs, enrollment shortfalls, emergency situations, and unbudgeted opportunities that come up during the year.

content.title: Zero-Based vs. Incremental Budgeting Approaches
content.text:
Schools may choose different approaches to budget development:

Incremental Budgeting starts with the previous year's budget. It then adjusts for inflation, enrollment changes and new programs. This approach is simpler and faster. It keeps resource allocation stable and needs less detailed justification. However, it may keep inefficiencies in place, fail to move resources from lower to higher priorities, and lack strategic alignment.

Zero-Based Budgeting requires every expense to be justified from zero each year, whatever the previous allocations were. Each program or department must present a case for resources based on expected outcomes and strategic priorities. This approach encourages strategic thinking and finds inefficiencies and low-value activities. It moves resources to the highest priorities and promotes new ideas and fresh thinking. However, it takes more time, may create uncertainty for department heads, and needs detailed data on program costs and outcomes.

**Recommended Approach:** Most Eduversal Partner Schools benefit from a modified zero-based approach. Core operating expenses (fixed costs like salaries, utilities, mandatory fees) get incremental treatment. Discretionary program budgets get a zero-based review every 2-3 years. This balances efficiency with strategic flexibility.

content.title: Enrollment Projections and Financial Modeling
content.text:
Budget development must begin with realistic enrollment projections, because tuition revenue usually makes up 80-90% of school income. Several factors shape the enrollment projection. These are historical retention rates (usually 85-95% in stable schools) and new student recruitment targets. Others are grade-level capacity limits, population trends in the school's catchment area, and competition with other international schools. Economic conditions that affect whether families can afford international education also matter. Principals should work with the admissions team and GM to project enrollment based on these factors.

Conservative enrollment projections protect financial sustainability. Budget scenarios should model best-case, expected-case and worst-case enrollment, with matching revenue and spending adjustments.

content.title: Contingency Planning
content.text: Careful financial management requires planning for bad scenarios. Schools should keep contingency reserves and make contingency plans for the following situations. One is an enrollment shortfall: what expenses can be reduced if enrollment is 5-10% below projection? Others are unexpected major expenses (facility emergency, equipment breakdown) and economic downturns that affect fee collections. The last is regulatory changes that need extra investments.

Once the draft budget is ready, it goes through a formal approval process. This process involves both Yayasan parties and makes clear who is accountable for carrying out the budget. Yayasan Approval Process and Timeline: As set out in the partnership technical guidelines (Juknis), the budget approval process follows these formal steps:

steps: The GM/Foundation Representative prepares the draft RAB in consultation with Eduversal and the Principal
The draft RAB is formally submitted to the Yayasan Board for evaluation

The Yayasan Board reviews the budget. It assesses financial assumptions and checks alignment with the school mission and strategic priorities. It reviews major spending categories and their justifications, and examines revenue projections and the tuition structure. It also makes sure the budget complies with Indonesian foundation law and accounting standards
The Yayasan Board approves the RAB or requests revisions and clarifications
The GM/Foundation Representative formally signs the final approved budget on behalf of school management. Both Yayasan parties (Eduversal and the local Yayasan partner) approve it
The approved budget is carried out according to the agreed plan. Any later changes require mutual consultation and agreement (musyawarah mufakat) between both parties
content.title: 13.2.2 Budget Approval and Oversight
Eduversal Quality Assurance Review
content.text: At the same time as the Yayasan review, Eduversal carries out a quality assurance review of partner school budgets. This review checks consistency with network-wide standards and checks the budget lines for QMS components (DTP, Appraisal, EduNav, EASE). It also assesses financial sustainability indicators, identifies possible risks or red flags, and shares best practices across the network. This dual review reflects the balanced governance structure of the partnership model. The Yayasan reviews for ownership accountability, and Eduversal reviews for educational quality.

content.title: Board Presentation Requirements
content.text: When presenting the budget to the Yayasan Board, the GM and Principal should prepare full materials. These include an executive summary of key budget drivers and strategic priorities, and a detailed budget by category with year-over-year comparisons. They also include enrollment projections and revenue assumptions, major program initiatives and their costs, and capital expenditure plans. Other items are financial sustainability metrics (operating margin, revenue per student, days cash on hand) and answers to likely Board questions or concerns. Clear, transparent communication builds trust. It also helps the Board take a constructive part in financial stewardship.

content.title: Monthly Monitoring Procedures
content.text:
Budget approval is not the end of financial management. It is the beginning. Good budget oversight requires regular monthly monitoring. This includes monthly financial reports that compare actual and budgeted revenue and expenses. It includes variance analysis that explains significant differences (typically ±5% or more) and trend analysis that identifies new patterns. It also includes updated forecasts of year-end results based on year-to-date performance, and action plans for worrying variances.

The finance team prepares these monthly reports, and the GM and Principal review them. The reports are shared with the Yayasan Board (usually as a quarterly summary). They are also uploaded to EduNav for transparency and documentation.

content.title: Variance Analysis Protocols
content.text:
When actual financial results differ significantly from the budget, principals must understand the causes and take appropriate action. Variance analysis separates favorable variances (revenue above budget or expenses below budget) from unfavorable variances (revenue below budget or expenses above budget). It shows whether variances are temporary timing differences or permanent changes in the underlying assumptions. It also shows whether variances are controllable (management can take action) or uncontrollable (external factors). This guides decisions about whether corrective action is needed.

For example, suppose curriculum resource spending is 15% over budget at mid-year. Variance analysis might show that textbook orders were front-loaded into the first semester (a timing difference). It might show that new curriculum materials required unbudgeted purchases (controllable through better planning). Or it might show that Cambridge changed examination specifications, so new materials were needed (an uncontrollable external factor). Each cause calls for a different management response.

content.title: Budget Adjustment Procedures (Mid-Year Revisions)
content.text:
Mid-year budget revisions may be necessary when circumstances change significantly during the year. Common triggers include enrollment that is significantly different from the projection, and unexpected facility emergencies that need major repairs. Other triggers are regulatory changes that impose new requirements, opportunities for major program improvements, or ongoing variances that show the original assumptions were wrong.

Mid-year budget adjustments must follow the same collaborative process as the first budget approval. In this process, management proposes revisions with clear justification. Both Yayasan parties discuss the revisions through consultation (musyawarah). The adjustments are formally approved and documented. The adjusted budget then becomes the new baseline for monitoring.

Principals should avoid two mistakes. One is treating the budget as endlessly flexible, because frequent revisions weaken financial discipline. The other is rigidly following an outdated budget when circumstances have changed, which is counterproductive.

content.title: 13.2.3 Revenue Management
content.text: Good revenue management keeps the school financially sustainable. It needs careful attention to several income streams, to fee collection, and to legal compliance.

content.title: Tuition Fee Structure and Collection
content.text:
At Eduversal Partner Schools, tuition is usually 80-90% of total school income. This makes good tuition management critical to the school's financial health. The tuition fee structure should reflect the educational value the school offers, while staying competitive in the local market for international education.

Factors that affect tuition levels include the school's market position compared with other international schools in the area. They also include the cost structure (personnel, Cambridge fees and QMS components) and value-added services (boarding, transportation, extracurricular programs). Other factors are what families in the target group can afford and the school's strategic financial sustainability needs.

Tuition fees usually have several parts. Base tuition covers the core teaching program and the Cambridge curriculum. Registration fees are one-time or annual enrollment charges. Development fees or capital assessments pay for facility improvements and major investments. Cambridge examination fees are passed on to families, sometimes with an administrative markup added by the school.

As part of their tuition policy, schools may offer sibling discounts, early payment incentives, or financial aid based on merit or need.

content.title: Payment Plans and Financial Aid Administration
content.text:
Schools usually offer set payment options. These help families afford the fees and keep the school's cash flow stable. The options include annual payment in advance (often with a 3-5% discount) and semester plans (two installments per year). They also include quarterly plans (four installments) and monthly plans (10 or 12 installments).

Each payment plan should state clearly the due dates, the late payment penalties (typically 1-2% per month), and the consequences of continued non-payment. These consequences are limited to the collection tools permitted in 13.2.3: payment plans, late fees, and suspension of optional services. They never include withholding report cards, transcripts, certificates, examination entries, or attendance.

When a school offers financial aid or scholarships, the program requires clear policies and transparent administration. This includes published eligibility criteria, application and document requirements, and a method for assessing need. It also includes a timeline for telling families about awards, renewal procedures, and confidentiality protections.

Financial aid should be budgeted as a reduction of gross tuition revenue, not as an expense line item.

content.title: Ancillary Revenue Streams
content.text:
Beyond tuition, schools may earn extra revenue from other sources that support financial sustainability:

**Uniform sales:** Many schools run uniform programs themselves or through vendor partners. Uniform revenue should cover costs plus a reasonable amount for administration. Some schools include basic uniform sets in tuition; others sell them separately.

**Transportation services:** School bus services may be included in tuition, offered as an optional extra, or run on a cost-recovery basis. Transportation revenue should cover vehicle operations, maintenance, insurance, driver salaries, and administrative costs. See Section 13.5 for full guidance on transportation management.

**Boarding services:** For schools with residential programs, boarding fees are a significant source of revenue. They cover accommodation, meals, supervision staff, residential programs, and facility operations. Islamic boarding schools may set fees differently to reflect religious education components. See Section 13.5 for details on boarding operations.

**Cafeteria and food services:** Day schools usually offer a cafeteria, either à la carte or with prepaid meal plans. Revenue should cover food costs, labor, kitchen operations, and facilities. Some schools subsidize the cafeteria as a student service, not as a profit center.

**Extended day programs or after-school care:** Before- and after-school supervision, homework clubs, or enrichment programs can earn extra revenue. They also serve the needs of working families.

**Facility rental:** School facilities (auditorium, gymnasium, classrooms) may be rented to community organizations, other schools, or private groups during evenings, weekends, or school holidays. Rental policies should cover insurance, supervision, cleaning, and wear-and-tear on facilities.

**Summer programs or holiday camps:** Academic enrichment, sports camps, or special interest programs during school breaks can earn revenue. They also keep facilities in use when they would otherwise be empty.

**Fundraising events:** School fairs, gala dinners, charity auctions, or sponsored runs can add revenue and build community engagement. Clear policies should separate fundraising for general operations from fundraising for a stated purpose (scholarship fund, specific projects).

content.title: Enrollment Forecasting Impact on Budget
content.text:
Revenue projections depend heavily on enrollment forecasts. This makes enrollment management a core financial skill for principals. Enrollment forecasts should consider historical trends (three-year retention and attrition patterns) and demographics (birth rates, community growth, economic conditions). The same applies to competition (new schools opening, competitor tuition changes) and to how attractive the program is (reputation, curriculum offerings, facilities). It also applies to how well marketing works (inquiry conversion rates, strength of the admissions pipeline).

Conservative enrollment projections protect against revenue shortfalls. Best practice suggests budgeting enrollment at 95% of the expected number. This gives a revenue cushion if projections fall short, and extra room if enrollment is higher than expected.

content.title: Bad Debt Provisions and Collection Procedures
content.text:
Schools will not collect all the tuition they bill. Realistic budgeting requires a bad debt provision based on past experience. In a stable economy, 1-3% of accounts are usually uncollectible. This can be higher in an economic downturn. Bad debt provisions should be budgeted as reductions to gross revenue.

Good collection procedures balance financial accountability with care and understanding for each family's situation.

Recommended practices are as follows. Explain payment expectations clearly at enrollment. Send automated billing reminders before due dates. Follow up quickly on missed payments (within 3-5 days). Contact the family personally when an account is 30+ days overdue, and send a formal notice at 60+ days overdue. Apply late-payment fees under the published fee schedule. Negotiate a payment plan with families in temporary hardship. After due process, suspend optional services (for example, extracurricular programs, school transport, or cafeteria accounts) for seriously overdue accounts. Have clear policies on writing off uncollectible accounts; a write-off requires Yayasan Board approval.

**What schools must never do:** Report cards, transcripts, certificates, examination entries, and class attendance are never withheld or blocked because of unpaid fees. This protects student welfare and the school's duties to registered Cambridge candidates. The only permitted collection tools are payment plans, late fees, and suspension of optional services. The same rule is stated in Section 2.9 (Prohibited Practices) and Sections 11.4/11.8 (Late Payment Policy and Outstanding Balances).

Collection efforts should be recorded carefully in student financial records, kept appropriately confidential, and handled with cultural sensitivity suited to the Indonesian context.

content.title: Indonesian Tax Implications
content.text:
Revenue management must take into account the Indonesian tax obligations that affect the school's net financial position:

**Pajak Pertambahan Nilai (PPN) - Value Added Tax:** Educational services from formal educational institutions with operational permits are generally exempt from PPN under Indonesian tax law. However, other services (uniform sales, cafeteria, facility rentals) may be subject to PPN at the standard rate. The rate is currently 12% under UU No. 7/2021 (Harmonisasi Peraturan Perpajakan). Schools should consult qualified tax advisors to get the PPN treatment and exemption documents right.

**Pajak Penghasilan (PPh) - Income Tax:** Schools run as foundations (Yayasan) may have tax-exempt status for educational operations under certain conditions. However, non-educational income may be taxable. Monthly and annual tax reporting (SPT, the tax return) is required. Correct income classification is essential to keep the tax-advantaged status.

**Withholding Tax Obligations:** Schools must do three things. They withhold income tax (PPh 21) from employee salaries. They withhold tax (PPh 23) from certain vendor payments. They pay the withheld taxes to the tax authorities on the required schedules. These taxes pass through the school, but they still need careful administration.

Principals should work closely with qualified Indonesian accountants or tax advisors to stay fully compliant with tax rules. These rules can be complex and can change. Tax non-compliance can lead to large penalties and put school operations at risk.

content.title: 13.2.4 Expenditure Controls
content.text: Revenue management brings enough money into the school. Expenditure controls make sure that money is used efficiently, appropriately, and in line with educational priorities. Strong expenditure controls protect against fraud, waste, and misuse of funds, while keeping operations flexible.

content.title: Purchase Order and Approval Systems
content.text:
All spending at Eduversal Partner Schools must follow formal approval processes recorded in the EduNav platform. EduNav gives transparency, accountability, and an audit trail for all financial transactions. The standard approval workflow in EduNav has four stages:

**Stage 1 - Initial Request:** The unit head or department coordinator responsible for a program area submits a purchase request through EduNav. The request states the item description, quantity, estimated cost, vendor (if known), and budget category. It also states the educational reason and the urgency or timeline. This first stage makes sure that requests come from the people who know the operation and are responsible for the program.

**Stage 2 - Department Review:** The request goes to the relevant department head or vice principal for review. The reviewer checks that the request fits departmental priorities and that budget is available in the relevant category. The reviewer also confirms that the expense is appropriate and necessary, and considers whether an alternative might be more cost-effective. The reviewer then either approves the request to move forward or returns it for clarification or revision.

**Stage 3 - GM/Foundation Representative Approval:** Approved requests go to the GM for final authorization. The GM checks that the request fits the overall school budget and strategic priorities. The GM also checks compliance with Yayasan policies and spending authorities, and confirms that proper procurement procedures will be followed. The GM considers the impact on cash flow and the financial position. The GM then either authorizes the purchase or asks for extra information or alternative proposals.

**Stage 4 - Financial Processing:** After GM approval, the request goes to the finance department. Finance makes the purchase, pays according to vendor terms, records and allocates the cost correctly, and keeps the documents. The finance team issues payment but has no authority to approve the educational or operational merit of purchases. That authority belongs to educational leaders.

This multi-stage process balances efficiency with oversight. Spending gets the right level of review without becoming too bureaucratic.

content.title: Spending Authority Levels
content.text: Clear spending authority levels prevent delays and still keep the right oversight. A typical authority matrix might include:

items: **Unit heads/coordinators:** Up to Rp 2,000,000 for routine supplies and materials within approved budgets (the department head is notified)
**Department heads/vice principals:** Up to Rp 10,000,000 for departmental needs within approved budgets
**Principal:** Up to Rp 25,000,000 for school operations within approved budgets (with GM notification)
**GM/Foundation Representative:** Up to Rp 50,000,000 for authorized expenditures within approved budget

**Yayasan Board approval required:** All spending over Rp 50,000,000, and any spending outside approved budget categories. Also all capital spending (regardless of amount), any spending that creates multi-year commitments, and all contracts longer than one year.

content.text: These thresholds should be adjusted to fit the school's size, complexity, and Yayasan policies. The key principle is that larger spending, and spending outside approved plans, requires higher-level authorization.

content.title: Procurement Procedures
content.text:
Procurement procedures make sure there is fair competition, value for money, and the right choice of vendor. They also prevent corruption and favoritism.

**Routine purchases (under Rp 10,000,000):** Unit heads may choose vendors based on past experience, quality needs, and competitive prices. The reason for choosing a vendor should be recorded. For items bought often, schools may set up preferred vendor lists with pre-negotiated prices.

**Significant purchases (Rp 10,000,000 - Rp 50,000,000):** Where practical, the school should get informal competitive quotes from at least three vendors. Price alone should not decide the choice; quality, service, delivery time, warranty, and vendor reputation should also be evaluated. The reasons for the selection should be recorded in the purchase request.

**Major purchases (exceeding Rp 50,000,000):** A formal competitive bidding process should be followed. It includes written specifications and formal quote requests to several qualified vendors. Bids are evaluated against criteria set in advance, and the Yayasan Board approves based on the documented evaluation. For very large purchases (facilities, major systems), professional procurement help may be advisable.

**Emergency purchases:** Urgent operational needs can arise (facility emergencies, health and safety issues, equipment breakdowns affecting teaching). In these cases, a faster approval procedure may be used, with documents and justification provided afterward. However, poor planning should not routinely be excused as an "emergency."

content.title: Vendor Management and Contract Oversight
content.text: Good vendor relationships support operational quality and cost control. Principals should build a systematic approach to vendor management. This includes the following steps. Keep a database of qualified vendors in key categories (curriculum suppliers, technology vendors, facilities contractors, food service, transportation). Review vendor performance regularly (quality, timeliness, service, responsiveness). Negotiate favorable terms (volume discounts, payment terms, service levels). Make sure contracts clearly state deliverables, timelines, acceptance criteria, and dispute resolution procedures. Monitor contract compliance for the whole contract period.

content.title: Eduversal Network-Wide Vendor Partnerships
content.text:
Eduversal has partnerships with several preferred vendors that give advantages to all partner schools. PT. Edukasi Universal Indonesia delivers DTP and the Appraisal Program. PT. Global Zerone Digital/Zerone provides the EduNav school information system and the Latihan.id assessment platform, through which EASE is delivered. Bess Project provides educational furniture, equipment, and supplies. Praktik Tour provides educational travel services.

These network-wide partnerships often give better prices because the network buys in volume. They also give quality assurance, because Eduversal checks the vendors, and consistency across the school network. Principals should give priority to these preferred vendors where appropriate. They can still use local vendors when that brings an advantage.

content.title: Cash Flow Management
content.text:
A school can have an approved budget and enough annual revenue and still face cash flow problems. This happens when money comes in and goes out at different times. Good cash flow management requires the following. Monitor the cash position every month. Project cash receipts from the tuition payment schedules. Time major spending to match the cash available. Keep a minimum operating cash reserve (typically 1-2 months of operating expenses). Tell the Yayasan when cash flow pressure appears. Consider negotiating payment terms with major vendors so payments better match the cash available.

Some schools have significant enrollment, and so large tuition receipts, at the start of each semester. These schools usually have their strongest cash position in July and January. Cash may get tighter in the later months of each semester. Expenditure planning should reflect these patterns.

content.title: Bank Account Management and Signatory Requirements
content.text:
School bank accounts hold significant financial assets and need proper safeguards. Best practices are as follows. Keep separate accounts for operating funds, restricted funds (if any), and payroll. Require two signatures for payments above a set threshold (e.g., Rp 25,000,000). Limit check signing authority to the GM and named senior administrators. Reconcile bank accounts regularly (at least monthly). Review bank statements for unauthorized transactions. Keep clear documents for all transactions.

Indonesian banking regulations and Yayasan policies may set specific requirements for account management, authorized signatories, and financial controls.

content.title: PPN and the education exemption
content.text:
Verified against UU No. 7/2021 (Harmonisasi Peraturan Perpajakan), read directly from the salinan. There are three points, and the third changes what schools were told before.

(1) RATE. Pasal 7(1) sets PPN at 11% from 1 April 2022, rising to 12% no later than 1 January 2025.

(2) WHAT COUNTS AS EDUCATION. The elucidation defines jasa pendidikan as the provision of school education and of out-of-school education. School education here means general, vocational, special, religious, academic and professional education. Tuition for the school program falls within this definition.

(3) THE LEGAL BASIS CHANGED. UU 7/2021 rewrote Pasal 4A(3), the list of services not subject to PPN. The education entry there now reads "dihapus" (deleted). The same is true for health, social, financial, insurance, transport and labor services. Education now appears instead in the strategic list at Pasal 16B(1a). There, tax may be "tidak dipungut sebagian atau seluruhnya atau dibebaskan", and the detail is "diatur dengan Peraturan Pemerintah". In practice, school fees still receive relief. But the relief now comes from Pasal 16B and its implementing regulation, not from an automatic exemption in Pasal 4A. So a statement that education is exempt "under Pasal 4A" now points to a deleted provision.

STILL FOR THE SCHOOL TO CONFIRM. Two points depend on implementing regulation and on the school's own situation. The first is how non-tuition income is treated, such as facility rental, catering, uniform sales and trips. The second is the surplus-reinvestment condition attached to income-tax relief for a yayasan. The finance office must confirm both with the school's tax adviser and record the date of that advice here. Do not treat non-tuition income as covered by the education relief without that advice.

content.title: Key Evidence and Artifacts — Financial Reporting and Accountability
13.3.1 Internal Financial Reporting
content.text: Internal financial reports give management and governing bodies timely information. They use this information to oversee the school and make decisions during the academic year.

content.title: Monthly Reports to Yayasan Board
content.text:
The Yayasan Board is the school's final fiduciary authority (it holds the school's resources in trust). It needs regular financial updates to carry out its governance duties. Monthly financial reports to the Yayasan usually include:

Financial Position Statement: It shows current assets (cash, accounts receivable, prepaid expenses) and current liabilities (accounts payable, deferred tuition revenue, accrued expenses). It also shows the net position or fund balance. This snapshot shows the school's financial health at one point in time.

Income Statement (Profit & Loss): It compares actual revenue and expenses with the budget, for the current month and for the year to date. Key sections are tuition and fee revenue by category, and ancillary revenue (boarding, transportation, other). They also include personnel expenses (salaries, benefits, taxes), operating expenses by major category, and the net operating surplus or deficit.

Cash Flow Statement: It tracks cash received from tuition, fees and other sources. It also tracks cash paid out for operations, payroll and capital purchases, and the opening and closing cash balances. Cash flow analysis shows the school's liquidity: its ability to meet short-term obligations.

Variance Analysis: It explains significant differences between actual and budgeted amounts (typically ±5% or ±Rp 5,000,000, whichever is greater). Variance explanations should cover three points. These are the cause (enrollment differences, timing, unbudgeted needs, operational changes), whether the variance is temporary or permanent, and any corrective actions needed.

Key Metrics Dashboard: It presents critical financial indicators. Examples are enrollment vs. projection, revenue per student, operating margin percentage, and days cash on hand. Others are accounts receivable aging (overdue tuition) and payroll as a percentage of revenue. These metrics give a quick view of financial trends.

Narrative Commentary from the GM/Foundation Representative: It explains the context of the financial data and highlights significant developments, risks or opportunities. It also recommends any actions that need Board consideration or approval.

The finance team usually prepares the monthly reports. The GM and Principal review them, and they go to the Yayasan Board within 10-15 business days after month-end. Some Yayasan Boards review monthly reports by email and discuss them formally at quarterly meetings. Others hold monthly Board finance committee meetings for a detailed review.

content.title: Quarterly Reports to Eduversal
content.text:
Eduversal requires quarterly financial reports from all partner schools. It uses them to monitor financial health across the network, find schools that need extra support, and compare financial performance across schools. It also uses them to compile consolidated financial information for Eduversal itself.

Quarterly reports to Eduversal usually include summary financial statements. These are less detailed than the monthly Yayasan reports, but they cover the major categories. They also include enrollment data and trends, key financial metrics and KPIs, and variance analysis for major differences from budget or prior year. Finally, they highlight significant developments or challenges and include any requests for Eduversal support or guidance, if needed.

These reports help Eduversal meet its partnership responsibilities. At the same time, Eduversal respects each school's autonomy under the Yayasan-Eduversal governance framework.

content.title: Principal's Financial Review Responsibilities
content.text:
The GM/Foundation Representative holds the main authority for financial management. However, the Principal also has important financial review duties. The Principal regularly reviews budget-to-actual reports for the areas the Principal oversees. The Principal checks that academic resources (curriculum materials, teaching supplies, student support services) are properly funded and delivered. The Principal approves departmental expense requests within the Principal's authority levels. The Principal identifies new financial concerns that may affect educational programs. The Principal also works with the GM on budget adjustments or decisions to reallocate resources.

The Principal is an educational voice in financial discussions. The Principal makes sure that budget decisions support student learning and wellbeing in the end, and do not become purely accounting exercises.

content.title: Key Financial Metrics and KPIs (tracked in EduNav)
content.text:
EduNav's financial dashboard gives real-time access to key performance indicators. These show the school's financial health and how efficiently it operates:

**Revenue Metrics:** Tuition revenue per student. Percentage of tuition collected vs. billed. Bad debt ratio (uncollectible accounts as % of revenue). Ancillary revenue per student (boarding, transportation, etc.)

**Expense Metrics:** Personnel cost ratio (total personnel expenses as % of revenue; typically 50-65%). Operating cost ratio (non-personnel operating expenses as % of revenue). Cost per student (total expenses divided by enrollment).

**Liquidity Metrics:** Days cash on hand (current cash balance divided by average daily expenses; target typically 30-60 days). Current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities; target >1.0). Accounts receivable aging (percentage >30, >60, >90 days overdue).

**Operating Performance:** Operating margin (net operating surplus/deficit as % of revenue; a positive margin is essential for sustainability). Budget variance (actual vs. budget; target ±3% annually). Break-even enrollment (the minimum enrollment needed to cover fixed costs).

These metrics help leaders manage finances early, instead of reacting to a crisis. Principals and GMs should review EduNav financial dashboards at least weekly, with formal monthly analysis and Yayasan reporting.

content.title: Format and Content Requirements
content.text:
Financial reports should follow a consistent format. This makes it easy to compare time periods and helps the Yayasan Board review the reports. Key formatting principles include clear labels for the report period and the date prepared. Categories stay the same from month to month and year to year. Side-by-side columns show the current period, the budget and the prior year. Reports use both absolute amounts (IDR) and percentages for key ratios. Visual indicators (color coding, charts, graphs) help readers see patterns quickly. An executive summary goes on the first page, with details in supporting schedules.

Reports should look professional, be free from errors, and be easy to understand for Board members who may not have financial expertise. Technical accounting terms should be explained when they are used.

content.title: Distribution and Confidentiality Protocols
content.text:
Financial reports contain sensitive information and need careful handling. Distribution usually works as follows. Board members receive full detailed reports. Eduversal receives quarterly summary reports. The Principal receives all reports related to school operations. Department heads receive information relevant to their areas. Access to detailed reports is restricted: they are not shared with general staff or outside parties without explicit authorization.

Confidentiality protections should cover four areas. These are secure transmission methods (encrypted email, password-protected files) and limited paper copies with controlled distribution. They also include a ban on redistribution without permission, and secure storage and disposal of sensitive financial documents.

Transparency does not mean open public access to everything. Responsible financial governance requires a balance between accountability and confidentiality.

content.title: 13.3.2 External Reporting Requirements
content.text: Schools also have external reporting duties, beyond internal management reports. They must meet several reporting obligations to Indonesian authorities, accreditation bodies and other stakeholders.

content.title: Indonesian Tax Reporting
content.text:
Indonesian tax law gives schools that operate as foundations significant reporting duties:

**Annual Tax Return (SPT Tahunan):** All foundations must file an annual tax return (SPT Tahunan PPh Badan) by the deadline. The deadline is typically April 30 following the tax year. The return must be filed even if the foundation has tax-exempt status for its educational activities. It reports all income, deductible expenses, tax calculations and supporting documentation.

**Monthly Tax Withholding Reports:** Schools must file monthly reports for employee income tax withholding (PPh 21), vendor withholding (PPh 23), and VAT/PPN (if applicable). These returns are typically due by the 20th of the following month. Accurate monthly reporting stops tax compliance problems from building up.

**Supporting Documentation:** Tax filings must be supported by detailed records. These include salary registers and PPh 21 calculations, vendor payment records and withholding certificates, and expense receipts and invoices. They also include asset registers for depreciation calculations, and bank statements and reconciliations. Indonesian tax authorities may audit schools and ask for supporting documents from several years back. Careful record-keeping is therefore essential.

**Tax Implications of Educational vs. Non-Educational Activities:** A foundation's educational activities generally receive favorable tax treatment. However, ancillary commercial activities (cafeteria, uniform sales, facility rentals) may be taxable. Correct classification and separate accounting for these activities are important. Schools should work with qualified Indonesian tax consultants to stay compliant as tax regulations change.

content.title: BAN-S/M Accreditation Financial Documentation
content.text:
Indonesian national accreditation (BAN-S/M) assesses schools against several standards, including financial management (Standard 8: Pembiayaan dan Pengelolaan). Schools preparing for an accreditation review must compile full financial documentation. This includes approved annual budgets for the past 3 years, and audited financial statements (if available) or detailed financial reports. It also includes evidence of transparent financial management processes, and Yayasan Board approval records for budgets and major spending. Other items are tuition fee schedules and financial aid policies, asset inventories and facility maintenance records, and evidence of financial compliance with Indonesian regulations.

BAN-S/M assessors check whether the school has enough financial resources to support its educational program. They also check for transparent financial planning and oversight, appropriate internal controls, and compliance with regulatory requirements.

Well-organized financial records in EduNav make accreditation preparation faster and easier.

content.title: CIS/WASC Accreditation Evidence
content.text:
International accreditation through CIS (Council of International Schools) and WASC (Western Association of Schools and Colleges) requires extensive financial evidence that matches their standards:

**CIS Domain G (Premises, facilities, technology systems and auxiliary services):** Schools must show the following. Financial resources adequately support the educational program, and facilities are well maintained. Technology infrastructure is adequate, and learning resources are enough and up to date. Financial evidence includes budget documents that show resource allocation priorities, and facility maintenance spending records. It also includes investment in curriculum materials and technology, and multi-year financial planning.

**CIS Domain B (Governance, ownership and leadership), standard B3 (educational and financial strategic and operational planning):** This standard covers financial governance directly. It requires evidence of strategic financial planning aligned with the school's mission, and transparent budget development with stakeholder input. It also requires evidence of Board oversight and fiduciary responsibility, internal controls and audit procedures, and financial sustainability planning. Evidence includes strategic plans with financial components, and Board minutes that record financial oversight. It also includes internal control policies and procedures, audit reports and management responses, and financial projections and sustainability analysis.

**WASC Category D (Resource Management and Development):** WASC evaluates how well schools allocate resources to support student learning. It requires similar evidence: budgets aligned with the strategic plan, transparent resource allocation processes, adequate facilities and financial sustainability.

Schools pursuing international accreditation should organize financial evidence systematically in EduNav's evidence repository, mapped to specific accreditation standards. This organized approach turns accreditation from a heavy compliance task into a chance to show good financial stewardship.

content.title: Annual Audit Requirements
content.text:
Annual external audits are not required for all Indonesian schools. However, they are best practice for financial accountability. They are often required by Yayasan governing documents, international accreditation standards, and significant donors or funding sources. Annual audits are carried out by qualified external auditors (preferably auditors with experience of Indonesian school operations). The audit gives independent confirmation that financial statements are accurate and internal controls are effective. It also confirms that financial operations follow applicable regulations and that assets are properly protected.

The audit report gives the auditor's opinion on the financial statements and identifies any material weaknesses in internal controls. It also recommends improvements to financial systems and highlights areas of concern that need management attention.

content.title: Financial Transparency for Stakeholders
content.text:
Beyond legal requirements, schools have an ethical duty to share financial information appropriately with stakeholders. These include parents (who pay tuition), staff (whose livelihoods depend on the school's financial health), and the wider community.

Financial transparency practices include an annual financial summary in school publications or on the website. This summary highlights budget priorities, major achievements and the financial position. Other practices are explaining the tuition structure (what tuition pays for and how fees are set), and answering reasonable stakeholder questions about financial matters. A last practice is accountability for how donated funds are used for their designated purposes.

Transparency does not mean publishing detailed line-item budgets publicly. It means communicating honestly about financial priorities, challenges and stewardship.

content.title: Public Disclosure Obligations
content.text: Some Indonesian schools may have public disclosure duties, depending on their legal structure, funding sources or regulatory status. Schools that receive government subsidies (for example, BOS funds) must report on how they use those funds, following government requirements. Schools should check their specific disclosure duties with legal counsel or regulatory advisors.

content.title: 13.3.3 Audit Procedures
content.text: External and internal audits are key accountability tools. They protect the school, the Yayasan and stakeholders.

content.title: Annual External Audit Process
content.text:
The annual external audit usually follows a set timeline:

**Planning Phase (1-2 months before fiscal year-end):** The Yayasan Board or audit committee hires qualified external auditors and agrees on the scope and fees. It also provides preliminary information and schedules the audit fieldwork.

**Preparation Phase (1 month after fiscal year-end):** The school finance team prepares preliminary financial statements and gathers supporting documentation. It also completes preliminary reconciliations and prepares the schedules the auditors ask for.

**Fieldwork Phase (1-2 weeks):** Auditors visit the school to review financial records and documentation, and to test internal controls and compliance. They interview key staff (GM, Principal, finance staff) and examine physical assets and records.

**Reporting Phase (2-4 weeks after fieldwork):** Auditors prepare a draft audit report, and management reviews and responds to the findings. The final audit report is then issued, and the audit is presented to the Yayasan Board.

**Follow-Up Phase (ongoing):** Management carries out the audit recommendations, and the Board monitors progress. The improvements become part of ongoing operations.

content.title: Internal Audit Protocols (Eduversal QMS)
content.text:
Eduversal's Quality Management System (QMS) also includes internal audits, in addition to external financial audits. These internal audits examine both financial and operational systems. Eduversal staff or hired consultants may carry them out. They usually take place every year or every two years.

These audits check compliance with Eduversal policies and standards, and the effectiveness of internal controls. They also look at operational efficiency and best practices, and at how quality management systems are put into practice (EduNav usage, financial procedures, documentation standards).

Internal audits are developmental, not punitive. They aim to find opportunities for improvement and to share best practices across the school network.

content.title: Audit Preparation and Documentation
content.text:
Successful audits need thorough preparation. Schools need organized financial records, with all transactions properly documented and classified. They need complete bank reconciliations, with all accounts reconciled to bank statements. They need asset inventories, with physical checks that match the records. Other items are an accounts receivable aging report (a detailed list of outstanding tuition) and an accounts payable list (all vendor obligations documented). Schools also need payroll records (detailed documentation of all pay) and contract files (copies of all significant contracts and agreements). Finally, they need Board minutes (recording all major decisions) and compliance documents (tax filings, regulatory reports, licenses).

Well-kept EduNav records make audit preparation much easier, because the platform serves as one central evidence repository.

content.title: Management Response to Audit Findings
content.text:
Audit reports usually include findings that range from simple recommendations to serious weaknesses.

A professional management response has several steps. Management reviews each finding objectively, without becoming defensive, and ranks the findings by significance and risk. It develops specific action plans with timelines and responsibilities, and shares these plans with the Yayasan Board. It then carries out the corrective measures and documents their completion, so that it can be checked later.

Some findings may need immediate action, such as internal control weaknesses that create a fraud risk. Others may be dealt with step by step over time, such as efficiency improvements. The key is to acknowledge findings openly and to commit to continuous improvement.

content.title: Follow-Up and Corrective Action Plans
content.text:
Audit recommendations only create value if they are put into practice.

Good follow-up includes a formal corrective action plan in writing, with a named person responsible for each action and a target completion date. Progress is monitored at regular management meetings and reported to the Yayasan Board at regular intervals. Internal or external auditors then check that the actions have been completed effectively.

Schools should keep an audit follow-up tracker. For each recommendation, it records the person responsible, the target date, the current status and the completion documents.

content.title: Document Retention Requirements
content.text: Indonesian law and international best practice require schools to keep financial records for set periods. Recommended retention schedules include:

items: **Permanent Retention:** Audited financial statements, Board minutes approving budgets and major decisions, property deeds and major contracts, corporate formation documents
**Minimum 10 Years:** Tax returns and supporting documentation, payroll records, major vendor contracts
**Minimum 7 Years:** Bank statements and reconciliations, accounts receivable and payable records, expense receipts and invoices, general ledger and journals
**Minimum 3 Years:** Routine correspondence, purchase orders, routine operational records

content.text: Document retention applies to both paper and electronic records. EduNav's document repository helps schools keep records in a compliant way, with automatic organization and secure storage.
