content.text: Physical facilities have a direct effect on the quality of education, student safety and the school's reputation. Good facilities management makes sure buildings, grounds and equipment support learning. It also makes sure they meet Indonesian safety standards and international accreditation requirements.

content.title: 13.4.1 Facility Planning and Development
content.text: **Long-Term Facility Master Planning:** Schools should develop 5-10 year facility master plans that match enrollment projections and Strategic Plan goals (See Section 4). A master plan covers classroom capacity needs (Indonesian sarana-prasarana standard: 4.9 m² minimum per student). It covers specialized learning spaces: science laboratories that meet Cambridge practical requirements, libraries that support research and literacy, and ICT labs for digital learning. These spaces also include art and music rooms, and physical education facilities such as sports courts and fields. The plan also covers expansion or renovation priorities and accessibility improvements for inclusive education (reference Section 8). Finally, it covers estimated costs and funding strategies.

content.title: Indonesian Building Code Compliance
content.text: All facilities must comply with Indonesian building regulations (Peraturan Menteri PUPR). These cover structural safety standards, fire safety requirements, electrical system standards, plumbing and sanitation codes, and occupancy permits. Principals should keep up-to-date records of building compliance and work with the Yayasan on major facility projects that need permits and inspections.

content.title: Tropical Climate Considerations
content.text: Indonesia's tropical climate creates specific facility challenges that need active management. Monsoon preparation covers roof and drainage maintenance, protection of flood-prone areas, and moisture control systems. High humidity management covers good ventilation, mold prevention, and dehumidification in sensitive areas such as libraries and server rooms. Year-round HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) needs include reliable air conditioning for learning spaces and regular filter maintenance. The temperature range is 23-25°C, per health standards. Heat management covers enough shading, reflective roofing materials, and cross-ventilation where possible.

content.title: 13.4.2 Preventive Maintenance Programs
content.text: **Annual Maintenance Calendar:** Planned preventive maintenance reduces costly emergency repairs and makes facilities last longer. The recommended annual maintenance schedule includes:

items: **Pre-Monsoon (September-October):** Inspect and repair roofs, clean the drainage system, clear gutters and downspouts, check window and door seals, check electrical grounding
**Mid-Year (December-January):** Service the HVAC system and replace filters, test the fire safety system, inspect emergency lighting, check playground equipment for safety, maintain landscaping

**Pre-Academic Year (May-June):** Deep-clean all facilities, repair and paint classroom furniture, inspect and calibrate laboratory equipment, maintain sports facilities, check technology infrastructure
**Quarterly (Throughout Year):** Pest control treatments, plumbing inspections, electrical panel checks, security system testing, building walk-throughs

content.title: Routine Inspection Protocols
content.text: Daily, weekly and monthly inspection checklists help find problems early. Custodial staff walk through the school daily and note visible issues. Coordinators inspect their assigned areas weekly. Management tours the facilities monthly, and a full facility audit takes place every year.

content.title: Equipment Maintenance Logs
content.text: All major building systems and equipment should have maintenance logs in EduNav. Each log records service dates, work done, parts replaced, costs and the next service due date. This tracking prevents equipment failure and supports warranty claims.

Work Order System: All maintenance requests should go through a formal work order system (usually in EduNav or separate facilities management software). The system records the requester's name and the date, the location and the exact problem, and the urgency level (emergency, high, medium, low). It also records the assigned maintenance staff or contractor, the completion date and work done, and the costs. Prioritization Criteria:

items: Emergency (immediate response): Safety hazards, complete facility system failures, security breaches
High Priority (24-48 hour response): Partial system failures that affect teaching, health concerns, significant water leaks
Medium Priority (3-7 day response): Repairs that are not critical but affect comfort or appearance, equipment maintenance
Low Priority (planned maintenance): Improvements to appearance, minor repairs that do not affect operations
content.title: 13.4.3 Reactive Maintenance and Emergency Repairs

content.text: Emergency Response Protocols: Facility emergencies require immediate action, coordinated with crisis management procedures (See Section 15.2). Emergency contacts for utilities, contractors and key administrators should be easy to find. After-hours emergency procedures should name on-call staff who have the authority to call in emergency services.

content.title: 13.4.4 Health and Safety Compliance
content.text: **Fire Safety Systems:** Indonesian fire safety regulations require working fire alarms and detection systems and enough fire extinguishers (inspected annually). They also require clear evacuation routes and signs, and emergency lighting. In addition, they require regular fire drills (minimum twice per academic year) and documented fire safety training for staff.

content.title: Building Safety Inspections
content.text: Regular inspections should cover: structural integrity; electrical safety (no exposed wiring, proper grounding, enough capacity); stairwell and railing safety; floor conditions (no trip hazards); ceiling and roof stability; and hazardous materials storage (chemicals in locked, ventilated areas with proper labeling).

content.title: Water Quality and Sanitation
content.text: Schools must ensure: safe drinking water, with regular testing (especially critical in boarding schools); enough toilet facilities (separate for boys, girls and staff, with proper ventilation); hand-washing stations with soap; waste management and disposal systems; and pest control (especially critical in a tropical climate).

Asset Registry System: All school assets should be tracked in a full register (EduNav or a spreadsheet). The register records a unique asset ID/tag number, a description and specifications, and the location. It also records the purchase date and cost, supplier/warranty information, the depreciation schedule, and the disposal/replacement date.

Physical Asset Tagging: Valuable assets should have physical identification tags. These tags help with annual physical inventories, discourage theft, and help with insurance claims.

Insurance Coverage: Full insurance should cover buildings and major infrastructure, furniture and equipment, valuable technology assets, and specialized equipment (science labs, sports facilities). Annual insurance reviews should check that coverage levels are enough.
content.title: 13.4.5 Asset Management

content.text: Transportation and boarding services extend the school's duty of care beyond the classroom. They need planned management to keep students safe and well.

content.title: 13.5.1 School Transportation Management
content.text: **Route Planning and Optimization:** Transportation routes should keep student travel time short and avoid dangerous roads or areas. The same applies to meeting the needs of special needs students and running at a reasonable cost. Annual route reviews should reflect enrollment changes.

content.title: Vehicle Fleet Management
content.text: School vehicles (owned or contracted) require proper licensing and full insurance, including passenger coverage. They also require regular maintenance schedules, safety inspections per Indonesian regulations, cleanliness standards, and emergency equipment (first aid kits, fire extinguishers, emergency contact information).

content.title: Driver Requirements
content.text: All drivers must have a valid Indonesian driver's license (appropriate category) and a clean driving record. Background checks and safeguarding training (See Section 9) are also part of this requirement. So are first aid certification, route familiarity and training, and professional conduct expectations.

content.title: Student Safety Protocols
content.text: Transportation safety requires assigned seating and attendance tracking, and seat belts where available. It also requires supervision by designated staff (for younger students) and emergency evacuation training. Other requirements are behavior expectations and disciplinary procedures, and parent communication systems (GPS tracking, arrival notifications).

content.title: Transportation Fee Structure
content.text: Transportation fees should cover vehicle operations and maintenance, driver pay, insurance, fuel costs, administrative oversight, and a contingency for unexpected repairs or fuel price increases.

content.title: 13.5.2 Boarding School Operations
content.text: **Residential Life Philosophy:** Boarding programs should state a clear educational philosophy. It connects residential life to the school mission and School Learning Outcomes. It balances structure with freedom suitable for the students' age, and builds community and character. It supports academic success through study time and homework support. It also integrates cultural values (for Islamic boarding schools, religious education and practices).

content.title: Boarding Staff Structure and Supervision
content.text: Good boarding requires enough staff. This includes residential supervisors/house parents, night duty staff, and weekday and weekend staffing. It also requires staff-to-student ratios suitable for the students' age (higher ratios for younger students). It requires clear reporting lines to the Principal and/or Director of Pastoral Care/Student Life, and links with the safeguarding framework (See Section 9).

content.title: Student Welfare and Pastoral Care
content.text: Boarding programs must provide 24/7 supervision and support, access to health services (an on-site clinic or protocols for medical needs), and counseling and emotional support. This duty also covers conflict resolution and peer mediation, and managing homesickness in younger students. It covers communication with parents (regular updates, scheduled call times, emergency contact protocols). It also covers attention to vulnerable students (younger, special needs, international).

content.title: Dormitory Management
content.text: Physical facilities require proper gender separation and privacy, age-appropriate grouping, and enough space per student (Indonesian standards). They also require climate control (especially important in a tropical climate), security systems and protocols, and regular maintenance and cleaning.

content.title: Meal Services and Nutrition
content.text: Boarding schools must provide three daily meals plus snacks, with balanced nutrition that meets growth needs. This duty also covers cultural dietary needs (halal for Islamic boarding schools) and special dietary needs (allergies, religious restrictions, medical requirements). It also covers food safety and hygiene standards, and meal schedules coordinated with the academic program.

content.title: Weekend and Holiday Programming
content.text: Boarding programs should plan structured weekend activities, study and enrichment programs, and a balance of rest and recreation. Their plans also cover excursions and cultural activities, and holiday arrangements (school closure periods, optional stay programs). They also cover clear communication to parents about schedules and expectations.

content.title: Islamic Boarding School Specifics
content.text: Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) include religious education in daily life. This covers daily prayer times (five daily prayers), Quranic studies and Islamic education, and Islamic ethics and character development. It also covers Ramadan programming (sahur and iftar arrangements, adjusted schedules) and Islamic values throughout residential life. Facilities should include proper prayer facilities (musholla or masjid), gender-separated living areas, and suitable supervision by religious educators.
Technology infrastructure makes modern teaching, learning and administration possible. Good IT management keeps systems reliable while controlling costs and security risks.

content.title: 13.6.1 IT Infrastructure Planning
content.text: **Technology Strategic Planning:** IT planning should align with the School Strategic Plan (Section 4) and support Cambridge digital learning initiatives. The same applies to budgeting 5-8% of the operating budget for technology and planning 3-5 year replacement cycles for major systems. It also applies to planning ahead for new educational technology needs.

content.title: Network Infrastructure
content.text: Reliable connectivity requires enough internet bandwidth (minimum 10 Mbps per 50 users, more for video/assessment) and strong WiFi coverage across the whole campus. It also requires network segmentation (admin, student, guest), backup connectivity options, and content filtering and monitoring.

content.title: Hardware Planning
content.text: Schools must address student computing access (computer labs, 1:1 devices, bring-your-own-device or BYOD policies) and teacher devices (laptops, tablets). The same applies to administrative workstations and classroom technology (projectors, interactive displays, audio systems). It also applies to specialized equipment (science data logging, design software, video production).

content.title: EduNav Platform Integration
content.text: All schools must keep active EduNav subscriptions and make sure staff are trained in EduNav and use it. The same applies to integrating financial and operational workflows, keeping data accurate and up to date, and using the evidence repository for accreditation.

Indonesian Data Protection: Schools must comply with the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP). Its requirements include consent for data collection, purpose limitation, secure storage and access controls, breach notification procedures, and data retention and deletion policies.

Cybersecurity Protocols: Essential security measures include firewalls and intrusion detection, regular software updates and patches, and strong password policies. They also include multi-factor authentication for sensitive systems, regular security audits, staff training on phishing and social engineering, and incident response plans.

Student Data Privacy: Particular care is required for student information. This includes academic records, health information, behavioral incidents, contact information, and photographs/videos. Access should be limited to legitimate educational purposes, with parent consent for data collection and use.
content.title: 13.6.2 Data Security and Privacy

content.text: Good procurement gets quality resources at reasonable costs. It also prevents corruption and favoritism.

items: Curriculum Resources: Cambridge-approved textbooks, digital resources, library materials, assessment materials
Technology: Hardware, software licenses, technical support services
Facilities: Maintenance contractors, cleaning services, landscaping, security
Food Services: Cafeteria/boarding meal suppliers (halal certification for Islamic schools)
Transportation: Vehicle suppliers, fuel, maintenance
Professional Services: Legal, accounting, consultants, educational services
content.title: 13.7.1 Key Vendor Categories

content.text: Eduversal Preferred Vendors: Network partnerships give better prices and quality assurance (PT Edukasi Universal Indonesia, PT Edukasi Aditama Indonesia, Zerone, Bess Project, Praktik Tour). Principals should use these partnerships and also keep local vendor relationships where they are useful.

Schools should keep full risk registers. These identify financial risks (enrollment shortfalls, bad debt, major unbudgeted expenses) and operational risks (facility failure, technology breakdown, staffing gaps). They also identify reputational risks (negative publicity, complaints, social media) and legal/compliance risks (regulatory violations, lawsuits). Finally, they identify health/safety risks (accidents, disease outbreaks, natural disasters).
content.title: 13.8.1 Operational Risk Management

content.text: Essential coverage includes property insurance (buildings, contents) and liability insurance (general, professional, directors & officers). It also includes student accident insurance, workers compensation (BPJS Ketenagakerjaan - Indonesian requirement), vehicle insurance, and business interruption insurance.
content.title: 13.8.2 Insurance Requirements

content.text: Schools should run energy conservation programs (efficient HVAC, LED lighting, solar where feasible) and water conservation (efficient fixtures, rainwater harvesting). The same applies to waste reduction and recycling, sustainable procurement, and environmental education as part of the curriculum.
content.title: 13.9.1 Environmental Initiatives

content.text: Environmental sustainability connects to the Indonesian value of gotong royong (community cooperation). It does this through school-community environmental projects, student environmental clubs, and campus greening initiatives. It also aligns with Profil Pelajar Pancasila (Berkebinekaan Global - Global Diversity competency).

subsections.title: Collaboration with the Yayasan and Eduversal

content.text: The Principal reports to the GM/FR on operational matters. The GM coordinates with the Yayasan Board and Eduversal. The Yayasan approves major decisions (budget, capital expenditures, strategic initiatives). Eduversal provides QMS (quality management system) support, network best practices, and technical assistance.
content.title: 13.11.1 Governance Framework

content.text: Eduversal offers finance consultation, procurement help, technology support, facilities planning expertise, and network learning opportunities. Principals should make active use of these resources.
content.title: 13.11.2 Support Services

content.text: Good operations and finance management is the essential foundation for excellent education. Key principles include:

items: **Mission Alignment:** Every operational decision must ultimately serve student learning and wellbeing.
**Transparency and Accountability:** Managing finances responsibly requires open communication, documented decisions, and responsible use of resources.
**Preventive Mindset:** Planned work and preventive maintenance prevent crises and reduce costs.
**Continuous Improvement:** Regular evaluation, benchmarking, and new ideas lead to excellent operations.
**Collaboration:** Good operations require partnership among the Principal, GM, Yayasan, Eduversal, and operational staff.
**Compliance Integration:** Indonesian regulations, Cambridge standards, and international accreditation requirements should be met through unified systems, not separate efforts.

content.text:
The guidance in Section 13 gives principals frameworks, procedures and practical tools to lead operations and finance well. With EduNav's digital infrastructure and Eduversal's network support, principals can achieve both operational efficiency and educational impact. These are the marks of excellent international schools.

**Resources Available:**

items: EduNav operational and finance modules
Eduversal consultation (finance, facilities, technology, procurement)
Network principal collaboration and best practice sharing
Templates and tools (budgets, reports, maintenance schedules, policies)
Professional development through DTP programs

content.text: Principals should remember that operational excellence is not a goal in itself. It is the way to create schools where teachers can teach well and students can learn with joy. In these schools, the whole community can pursue its educational mission without unnecessary obstacles.
